subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
They destroy all the host's T-cells
They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as HIV?
options: Viruses lack the metabolic processes and structures (e.g. cell walls, ribosomes) that antibiotics target
Viruses are too large to be affected
questions.explain: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes; viruses use host-cell machinery and lack these targets, so antibiotics do not affect them.

questions.q: HIV cannot replicate without a host cell because it:
options: Is too small to contain genetic material
Lacks the enzymes and ribosomes needed for protein synthesis and energy release
questions.explain: As a virus, HIV has no metabolic machinery of its own and must use the host cell's enzymes and ribosomes to replicate.

questions.q: A cell measures 30 mm in a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of x1500. The actual size of the cell is:
questions.explain: Actual size = image size / magnification = 30 mm / 1500 = 0.02 mm = 20 micrometres.

questions.q: A scanning electron microscope (SEM) is particularly useful for studying the surface of a pollen grain because it:
options: scans the surface and detects reflected/secondary electrons to build a 3D image of surface topography
uses visible light to give true colour
passes electrons through a thin section to show internal detail
questions.explain: An SEM scans the specimen surface, and detected secondary electrons produce a three-dimensional image of surface features.

questions.q: Meiosis produces:
questions.explain: Two successive divisions yield four haploid cells, each genetically unique due to crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.q: A plant cell becomes plasmolysed when placed in a concentrated salt solution because:
options: salt is actively pumped out of the cell
water enters the cell, pushing the membrane against the wall
water leaves the cell by osmosis, so the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall
questions.explain: The external solution has a lower (more negative) water potential, so water leaves the cell and the plasma membrane pulls away from the wall.

questions.q: When a B-cell is activated and divides, the process that produces many identical cells is called:
questions.explain: The selected B-cell divides by mitosis to form a clone of identical cells, some becoming plasma cells and others memory cells.

questions.q: The Golgi apparatus is mainly responsible for:
options: modifying, packaging and sorting proteins into vesicles for secretion
questions.explain: The Golgi modifies proteins (e.g. adding carbohydrate), packages them into vesicles and labels them for their destination.

questions.q: A plant cell at full turgor has a pressure potential of +600 kPa and a solute potential of -800 kPa. Its water potential is:
questions.explain: Psi = solute potential + pressure potential = -800 + 600 = -200 kPa.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, cytotoxic (killer) T-cells destroy infected body cells by:
options: Releasing perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane so the cell dies
questions.explain: Cytotoxic T-cells release perforin that perforates the membrane of infected cells, causing them to die before the pathogen can multiply.

questions.q: A plant cell with a water potential of -500 kPa is placed in a solution of water potential -300 kPa. The cell will:
options: gain water by osmosis because the solution has a higher (less negative) water potential
questions.explain: Water moves from higher to lower water potential, so water enters the cell (from -300 to -500), and the cell gains water and becomes more turgid.

questions.q: Cholesterol contributes to membrane stability at low temperatures by:
options: preventing the phospholipids from packing too closely, so the membrane does not become too rigid and stays fluid
allowing phospholipids to pack tightly and freeze solid
questions.explain: At low temperatures cholesterol stops phospholipids packing tightly together, maintaining fluidity and preventing the membrane becoming too rigid.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium across a membrane during diffusion:
options: molecules move only from low to high concentration
molecules continue to move in both directions but there is no net movement
questions.explain: At equilibrium molecules still move randomly both ways, but with equal rates so there is no net change in concentration.

questions.q: Which factor would increase the permeability of a cell membrane?
options: A decrease in temperature, increasing phospholipid order
An increase in temperature, increasing phospholipid movement and creating gaps
questions.explain: Higher temperatures increase phospholipid kinetic energy and fluidity, and can denature membrane proteins, increasing permeability.

questions.q: A glycoprotein on the cell-surface membrane functions mainly as:
options: a cell-surface receptor or recognition site for cell signalling and identification
questions.explain: Carbohydrate chains on glycoproteins act as recognition markers and receptors for hormones and in cell-to-cell recognition.

questions.q: The resolution of an electron microscope is greater than that of a light microscope because:
options: electrons travel more slowly than light
electrons have a longer wavelength than light
electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
the specimen is stained more heavily
questions.explain: Resolution depends on wavelength; the very short wavelength of an electron beam allows much finer detail to be distinguished.

questions.q: When a fully turgid plant cell has its pressure potential exactly balancing its solute potential, its water potential is zero, meaning:
options: there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell when surrounded by pure water
questions.explain: At full turgor the inward pressure potential equals the solute potential in magnitude, giving Psi = 0, so no net water movement occurs with pure water outside.

questions.q: Crossing over during meiosis:
options: occurs in anaphase II between sister chromatids
involves exchange of alleles between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at the chiasmata
reduces the chromosome number to haploid
questions.explain: In prophase I, non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange equivalent sections at chiasmata, producing new allele combinations.

questions.q: HIV is described as a retrovirus because it:
options: Contains RNA and uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA inside the host cell
questions.explain: HIV carries RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which produces DNA from the viral RNA so it can integrate into the host genome.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the cell cycle?
questions.explain: Interphase comprises G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (preparation), followed by mitosis and cytokinesis.

questions.q: Receiving an injection of antibodies (e.g. anti-tetanus serum) provides:
questions.explain: Ready-made antibodies are introduced artificially without the body making its own, giving immediate but short-lived (passive) protection.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, T-helper cells are activated when they:
options: Bind to antigens presented on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell
Bind directly to free antigens in the blood
questions.explain: T-helper cells have receptors complementary to antigens displayed by antigen-presenting cells, and this binding activates them.

questions.q: Why does an untreated HIV infection eventually leave a person vulnerable to opportunistic infections?
options: HIV destroys the bone marrow completely
The falling number of T-helper cells weakens both humoral and cell-mediated responses
questions.explain: As HIV depletes T-helper cells, the immune system can no longer coordinate effective responses, so normally harmless microbes cause disease.

questions.q: Cells specialised for absorption, such as the epithelial cells of the ileum, increase their rate of uptake by having:
options: fewer carrier proteins to reduce competition
microvilli that greatly increase the surface area of the membrane for transport proteins
questions.explain: Microvilli increase the membrane surface area, providing more sites for carrier and co-transport proteins and so faster absorption.

questions.q: Self-antigens normally do not trigger an immune response because:
options: Lymphocytes that would respond to the body's own antigens are destroyed or suppressed during development
They are too small to be detected
questions.explain: During development, lymphocytes complementary to self-antigens undergo clonal deletion or suppression, preventing autoimmune attack.

questions.q: A red blood cell placed in pure water bursts (haemolysis) because:
options: the membrane actively pumps water in
water enters down a water potential gradient and the cell has no rigid wall to resist swelling
water leaves the cell by osmosis
solutes enter the cell by active transport
questions.explain: Pure water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm, so water enters by osmosis; lacking a cell wall, the animal cell swells and lyses.

questions.q: Active transport differs from facilitated diffusion because active transport:
options: requires ATP to move substances against their concentration gradient via carrier proteins
moves substances down a concentration gradient
questions.explain: Active transport uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to pump substances against their gradient through carrier proteins.

questions.q: In cancer treatment, monoclonal antibodies can be used for 'targeted' drug delivery because they:
options: Convert cancer cells back to normal
Bind specifically to antigens on cancer cells, carrying an attached drug only to those cells
questions.explain: Antibodies specific to tumour antigens deliver a cytotoxic drug directly to cancer cells, reducing harm to healthy tissue.

questions.q: The clonal selection and activation of a specific B-cell typically requires:
options: Antigen binding plus stimulation by an activated T-helper cell releasing cytokines
Only the antigen binding to the B-cell receptor
questions.explain: Most B-cells require both antigen binding and signals (cytokines) from T-helper cells to divide and differentiate.
